{"self_assessment":"Impact: I chose the animal and the design. I proposed a large fish because its outline reads as a fish on its own, and I sketched it on the pad with the start at the nose, a top line and a belly line, and a forked tail. I laid the start domino and the whole top line, which carries the fall from the start round the head. By the end, about 123 of the 125 standing dominoes were connected to the start.

Execution: I laid the top line from the start round the head and added dominoes to round the tight nose turn so the fall could pass into the belly. When the top line and belly were falling toward the start, I bridged from the end of the belly line up into the top line so the fall could go round the whole fish. I then closed the gap where the upper tail meets the top line. I inspected the nose joint and the upper tail join several times, and nudged the dominoes that sat off the line until the picture was dark from the start. I stopped touching things once it was connected, to avoid bumping the table.

Collaboration: I split the work early. Maya took the belly line, Priya the tail, and Tom was asked to check joints and help with the belly. I asked people to stay clear of a spot while I worked on a joint, and I told the table when the top line had reached the nose so the belly could start there. In the last minutes I kept everyone hands off so nothing was knocked.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first minute, assigned strokes, and kept the team coordinated on one sketch. I kept attention on what the start would actually knock over. That caught the fall-direction problem at the join and the pale upper tail, and the team fixed both before the push. We finished with time to spare and a connected fish.","my_share_percent":40}
